screens.title: Advanced Data Fetching with Axios and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on a practical HTTP client that developers commonly choose when building medium and large React Native apps. Axios gives you readable request methods, automatic JSON parsing into response. data, and a richer error object that makes handling server and network failures easier. You will learn to install and configure Axios, use its convenience methods for GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE, and implement robust error handling so your UI can show precise messages. We will also cover interceptors: small functions that run before requests or after responses so you can add authentication headers, refresh tokens, or centralize logging. Finally, you'll see how to create custom Axios instances for different APIs, keeping code organized and preventing global configuration conflicts. As we go, I will point out common mistakes such as failing to inspect err. response versus err. request, or forgetting to await a call. By the end you will know when Fetch is sufficient and when Axios gives you practical advantages for maintainable code. Think about a real app you maintain: how would clearer error details change your user feedback and debugging speed?

Advanced Data Fetching with Axios

In this lesson
Coming up

Quick orientation
This chapter is practical. You will refactor a Fetch-based component to use Axios, add a request interceptor to attach a static header, confirm the header appears in network tooling, and centralize error handling using Axios's error object.
Why it matters
Better error objects and interceptors reduce boilerplate and improve debugging speed across your app.

Teams maintaining multiple APIs, authentication flows, or apps with complex error UX.
Explore Key Topics
Fetch vs Axios
Contrast error behavior and JSON handling to choose the right tool.
Interceptors
Add auth headers or central response handling for token refresh and logs.
Custom Instances

Richer errors

Interceptors
Request and response hooks that run globally or per instance to modify traffic.

Choose Axios when you need consistent error rejection, easy JSON access via response.data, and centralized request or response behaviors with interceptors and custom instances.

screens.title: Fetch versus Axios — practical differences
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare the two tools you can use for network requests. Fetch is built into the platform and handles basic requests well; it resolves the returned promise even for HTTP error statuses, which means you must manually check response. ok and parse JSON. Axios, by contrast, rejects the promise for non-2xx status codes and gives you an error object that often includes response, request, and message fields. That difference makes it easier to route errors: a server 500 will throw and land in your catch block with response. status available. Practically, if your app has simple read-only requests, Fetch may be sufficient and keep dependencies minimal. If you need consistent error semantics, convenience methods for each HTTP verb, or you want to centralize behaviors like adding an Authorization header across many calls, Axios streamlines that work. A common misconception is that Fetch is always faster because it's native; performance is rarely the deciding factor. Instead, the deciding factor is complexity: how many places in your app need identical header logic, token refresh, or consistent error handling. Example: when an endpoint returns 401, Axios will reject and provide error. response. status so you can redirect to login; with Fetch you must check the response and throw yourself. Takeaway: choose Fetch for minimal use cases and Axios when consistent error handling and centralized request behaviors will reduce duplicated code and bugs. How would this choice affect your current app's error paths?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Fetch vs Axios
Fetch
Native API for basic requests. Requires manual checks for HTTP status and explicit JSON parsing for each call.
When to choose
Small utilities or pages with a few simple fetches and no shared headers or global error handling.
Common pitfall
Assuming HTTP errors reject the promise leads to silent success paths unless you check response.ok.
Axios
A promise-based client that rejects for non-2xx statuses, parses JSON into response.data, and supports interceptors and custom instances.
When to choose
Apps with many endpoints, authentication needs, or centralized error handling across components.
Common advantage
Easier error inspection via err.response and simpler POST payload handling.
Key Takeaway

Pick Axios when consistent error semantics, interceptors, and organized instances reduce duplicated code; use Fetch for minimal, dependency-free scripts.

screens.title: What is Axios and how it helps
screens.narratorSegment: Axios is a promise-based HTTP client that runs in both browser and Node environments and is commonly used in React Native projects. At its core Axios provides named convenience methods for HTTP verbs, automatic parsing of JSON responses into response. data, and a richer error object that distinguishes server responses from network failures. Think of Axios as a small network middleware library: instead of repeating header setup and error parsing across many components, you use the same client with consistent behavior. Concretely, axios. post lets you pass a plain JavaScript object and Axios sets the Content-Type header and stringifies the body for you. A helpful analogy is a mailroom clerk: rather than every developer formatting envelopes and checking delivery receipts, Axios standardizes packaging and returns a status object you can inspect. A common misconception is that Axios hides HTTP entirely; it does not — it surfaces the same HTTP status codes, headers, and bodies but makes them easier to inspect and act on. Example: when a POST returns a created resource, use response. data directly to add it into state instead of parsing the body manually. Final takeaway: Axios reduces repetitive plumbing so you can focus on app logic and robust error handling.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is Axios
Axios — short definition
A promise-based HTTP client that simplifies requests, errors, and global behaviors for medium and large apps.
Automatic JSON
Use response.data instead of manual parsing.
Rejects on errors
Non-2xx statuses throw and land in catch blocks.
Interceptors
Run shared logic before requests or after responses.
Analogy: Axios as a mailroom
Rather than each developer wrapping data and checking receipts, Axios standardizes packaging and returns a structured delivery record you can act on. This reduces repeated plumbing across components.
Key Takeaway

Axios does not replace HTTP; it makes HTTP easier to use consistently across your app by reducing repeated setup and improving error inspection.

screens.title: Install and basic GET / POST with Axios
screens.narratorSegment: First, install Axios in your React Native project using the package manager you prefer. Once installed, import Axios and use its convenience methods. For a GET request, axios. get returns a promise whose resolved value holds parsed JSON under response. data. For a POST, you can pass a plain object as the body and Axios will set the appropriate header and stringify the payload. An important practical note: always await the axios call inside an async function so errors can be caught with try... catch. Below you will see two short code examples: a terminal install command and minimal GET and POST examples using Axios. The GET example fetches posts and assigns response. data to state. The POST example constructs a JavaScript object and sends it directly. A common mistake is manually calling JSON. stringify or forgetting headers; Axios handles those details for you. Try these snippets in a small screen that shows loading, error, and result states so you can observe response. data directly in your component state. After testing, confirm the network tool shows a request body and a Content-Type header set to application/json.

keyIdea.title: Practical setup
keyIdea.text: Install Axios, then use axios.get and axios.post with await; response.data is your parsed JSON result.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Install & Basic Requests
Install
npm install axios
# or
yarn add axios
GET example
<!-- in a React Native component -->
async function fetchPosts() {
  try {
    const response = await axios.get('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=10');
    // parsed JSON available at response.data
    setPosts(response.data);
  } catch (err) {
    // handle err.response / err.request / err.message
  }
}
POST example
async function createPost() {
  const newPost = { title: 'My New Axios Post', body: 'Content', userId: 1 };
  try {
    const response = await axios.post('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts', newPost);
    // response.data contains the created resource
  } catch (err) {
    // handle error
  }
}
Note: Axios sets Content-Type and stringifies the body automatically for JSON objects.
Check your understanding

Run the GET and POST in a small component, log response.data, and confirm the network tool shows the JSON body and Content-Type header.

screens.title: Advanced error handling with Axios
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling is one of Axios's biggest practical advantages. When a request fails, Axios may provide three different pieces of information: error. response, error. request, and error. message. error. response exists if the server replied with a status outside the 2xx range; it includes details like status, data, and headers so you can show a specific message for 401 or 500. error. request is present when a request was made but no response was received, indicating network failures or timeouts. error. message covers lower-level issues like misconfigured requests. A recommended pattern is to wrap every awaited call in try... catch and branch inside catch to handle these cases: for error. response read status to decide retry or sign-out flows; for error. request surface a network error UI; otherwise treat it as a request setup issue. A common mistake is checking only error. message or assuming all errors are network errors. Example: when err. response. status equals 401, prompt re-authentication; when err. request is truthy, show a network retry option. Close by logging error. response and error. request during development to learn what your backend returns. Takeaway: differentiate server errors from network and setup errors so your app can respond correctly and communicate useful feedback to users.

keyIdea.title: Error pattern
keyIdea.text: Inspect err.response first for server errors, then err.request for network failures, otherwise handle err.message as a setup or unknown issue.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Error Handling
Typical try...catch
try {
  const response = await axios.get(url);
  // use response.data
} catch (err) {
  if (err.response) {
    // server responded with status outside 2xx
    // use err.response.status and err.response.data
  } else if (err.request) {
    // request made but no response received
  } else {
    // request setup error
  }
}
During development, console.log err.response and err.request to learn backend behavior.
Handling examples
401 Unauthorized
If err.response.status === 401, prompt for sign-in or trigger token refresh logic.
No response
When err.request exists, surface a network retry UI and avoid showing misleading server messages.
Key Takeaway
Differentiate server, network, and setup errors and handle each with a targeted UX path.

screens.title: Interceptors — add headers and centralize behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Interceptors let you run functions globally before a request is sent or after a response is received. Use a request interceptor to attach headers like Authorization or a custom X-App-Version header, and use a response interceptor to inspect or transform responses and to catch specific status codes like 401 for re-authentication. The process is predictable: the request interceptor receives the config, you modify config. headers as needed, then return config. For responses, return the response to continue the promise chain or inspect error status codes in the response interceptor's error handler. A common use case is adding a request interceptor that reads a token from secure storage and sets the Authorization header. Another use case is logging response. status and response. config. url for telemetry. A key misconception is that interceptors run per component — they run on the Axios instance on which they were registered. That is why creating instance-specific interceptors keeps side effects scoped. Example: add a request interceptor that logs and attaches X-App-Version; then watch the network tool to confirm the header appears on each outgoing request. Final takeaway: interceptors centralize repetitive request and response work so components stay focused on state and rendering.

keyIdea.title: Interceptor pattern
keyIdea.text: Request interceptors modify config before sending; response interceptors inspect or transform results and handle cross-cutting errors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Interceptors
Request & response interceptors
Step through the common interceptor lifecycle and a typical use-case to attach a header.
1. Request interceptor
Receives config, optionally read token from storage, set config.headers.Authorization, return config.
2. Server processing
Server receives headers and body, returns a response or an error status code.
3. Response interceptor
Inspect response, transform data, or on error check status codes to trigger global logic like sign-out.
<!-- request interceptor example -->
axios.interceptors.request.use(async config => {
  const token = await AsyncStorage.getItem('userToken');
  if (token) config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${'{token}'}`;
  config.headers['X-App-Version'] = '1.0.0-rn';
  return config;
}, error => Promise.reject(error));
Key Takeaway
Register interceptors on the correct instance to limit side effects, and use them to centralize auth headers and response handling.

screens.title: Custom Axios instances for multiple APIs
screens.narratorSegment: When your app talks to more than one A P I or when some endpoints need different timeouts and headers, create a custom Axios instance rather than mutating global defaults. Use axios. create with options like baseURL, timeout, and default headers. Then register instance-specific interceptors to scope logging or auth to that A P I only. This prevents accidental side effects when other services require different behavior. For example, set baseURL to the A P I root and a five-second timeout for the users service. In code you import the configured instance and call api. get('/users') rather than axios. get with full URLs. This keeps components cleaner and makes tests simpler because each instance has predictable behavior. A common misconception is that axios. defaults is sufficient — it can be, but it mutates global state and makes isolation harder. Creating instances is a lightweight pattern that improves modularity and reduces unexpected interactions between modules. Try exporting an instance from an api. js file and swapping it into a component to see how code becomes shorter and configuration is centralized. Custom Axios instances for multiple APIs means use axios.create for per-api configurations so headers, timeouts, and interceptors remain scoped and predictable.. In practical terms, keep different api configurations isolated and clear. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instance principle
keyIdea.text: Use axios.create for per-API configurations so headers, timeouts, and interceptors remain scoped and predictable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Custom Instances
api.js example
import axios from 'axios';

const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: 'https://api.yourapp.com/v1',
  timeout: 10000,
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Accept': 'application/json' }
});

api.interceptors.request.use(config => config);
export default api;
Import this instance in components and call api.get('/users') instead of full URLs.
Why it matters
Instances keep configuration local, avoid global mutations, and allow instance-specific interceptors that only affect a single API surface.
Practical example
Create an instance for your public API and another for an internal service that requires extra headers or shorter timeouts.
Common mistake
Modifying axios.defaults spreads settings across all requests and makes isolation and testing harder.

screens.title: Refactor a Fetch component to Axios
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a small refactor from Fetch to Axios. The goal is to keep the component behavior identical while reducing parsing and error-checking boilerplate. Start with a component that calls fetch, checks response. ok, and then uses response. json. Replace that logic with a single await axios. get call and assign response. data directly to state. Also replace manual header setup in POSTs with axios. post and pass a plain object. When refactoring, pay special attention to error handling: convert explicit status checks to a try... catch where you inspect err. response and err. request. A typical mistake is forgetting to remove the old manual response. ok checks, leaving duplicated error branches. After refactor, test the UI loading and error states and confirm response. data contains the expected array or object. If your app needs a shared header, move that into an interceptor or into a custom instance so the component stays focused on rendering only. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor Demo
Before (Fetch)
async function fetchPostsWithFetch() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts');
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Network response was not ok');
    const data = await res.json();
    setPosts(data);
  } catch (err) {
    // handle errors
  }
}
After (Axios)
async function fetchPostsWithAxios() {
  try {
    const response = await axios.get('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts');
    setPosts(response.data);
  } catch (err) {
    // inspect err.response / err.request / err.message
  }
}
Notice the removal of manual ok checks and json parsing; response.data is ready to use.
Pro tip
After refactor, remove redundant error branches and move shared headers into an interceptor or instance.

screens.title: Timeouts, headers, and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Three configuration details often improve reliability: timeout, baseURL, and headers. Timeout cancels long-running requests; set it in an instance when endpoints are known to be slow. baseURL shortens component code and helps enforce the correct A P I root. Default headers set sensible Content-Type and Accept values so servers receive predictable requests. Common mistakes include forgetting to await an Axios call so errors are uncaught, checking only error. message and missing err. response data, or setting axios. defaults globally when you meant to scope settings to a single A P I. For each mistake, the remedy is straightforward: always await in async functions, check err. response and err. request inside catch, and use axios. create for per-A P I defaults. Example configuration in the chapter shows a five-second timeout for JSONPlaceholder; adjust timeouts for realistic server behavior. After applying these tips, test the app under slow network conditions and confirm the timeout behavior and header presence in your network instrumentation. These small improvements dramatically reduce intermittent bugs and make debugging reproducible. Configurations that matter
baseURL
Shortens calls and centralizes API root.
timeout
Automatically cancels excessively slow requests.
default headers
Set Content-Type and Accept consistently for the API.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on a practical HTTP client that developers commonly choose when building medium and large React Native apps. Axios gives you readable request methods, automatic JSON parsing into response. data, and a richer error object that makes handling server and network failures easier. You will learn to install and configure Axios, use its convenience methods for GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE, and implement robust error handling so your UI can show precise messages. We will also cover interceptors: small functions that run before requests or after responses so you can add authentication headers, refresh tokens, or centralize logging. Finally, you'll see how to create custom Axios instances for different APIs, keeping code organized and preventing global configuration conflicts. As we go, I will point out common mistakes such as failing to inspect err. response versus err. request, or forgetting to await a call. By the end you will know when Fetch is sufficient and when Axios gives you practical advantages for maintainable code. Think about a real app you maintain: how would clearer error details change your user feedback and debugging speed?

These objectives focus your practice and give clear, verifiable outcomes. First, you will explain the practical advantages of Axios over the native Fetch A P I, which helps you decide the right tool as an application grows. Second, you will install and configure Axios and use its convenience methods for GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE so you can write readable request code without manual JSON stringification. Third, you will implement advanced error handling strategies that check for error. response and error. request so your app can present precise feedback for server and network failures. Fourth, you will utilize Axios interceptors to add or refresh authentication headers and to centralize logging or error handling. Each objective has a small mnemonic to help you remember the workflow and a verified competency milestone to mark practical completion. Practice these objectives with the included starter code and the refactor activity to make them concrete.

These additional objectives extend configuration and practical checks. You will configure custom Axios instances with baseURL and timeout settings, which helps you separate A P I concerns and avoid global side effects. Next, you will rely on response. data as the primary source for parsed JSON in Axios responses, reducing boilerplate parsing. You will learn to apply instance-specific interceptors for logging and auth flows, keeping global defaults untouched. Finally, you will recognize common mistakes such as neglecting to check err. response versus err. request, or forgetting to await an Axios call. Practicing these objectives in the refactor activity will show how small changes produce clearer code and easier debugging. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to make recall easier and a verified competency milestone you can tick off after testing the starter project.

Let's compare the two tools you can use for network requests. Fetch is built into the platform and handles basic requests well; it resolves the returned promise even for HTTP error statuses, which means you must manually check response. ok and parse JSON. Axios, by contrast, rejects the promise for non-2xx status codes and gives you an error object that often includes response, request, and message fields. That difference makes it easier to route errors: a server 500 will throw and land in your catch block with response. status available. Practically, if your app has simple read-only requests, Fetch may be sufficient and keep dependencies minimal. If you need consistent error semantics, convenience methods for each HTTP verb, or you want to centralize behaviors like adding an Authorization header across many calls, Axios streamlines that work. A common misconception is that Fetch is always faster because it's native; performance is rarely the deciding factor. Instead, the deciding factor is complexity: how many places in your app need identical header logic, token refresh, or consistent error handling. Example: when an endpoint returns 401, Axios will reject and provide error. response. status so you can redirect to login; with Fetch you must check the response and throw yourself. Takeaway: choose Fetch for minimal use cases and Axios when consistent error handling and centralized request behaviors will reduce duplicated code and bugs. How would this choice affect your current app's error paths?

Axios is a promise-based HTTP client that runs in both browser and Node environments and is commonly used in React Native projects. At its core Axios provides named convenience methods for HTTP verbs, automatic parsing of JSON responses into response. data, and a richer error object that distinguishes server responses from network failures. Think of Axios as a small network middleware library: instead of repeating header setup and error parsing across many components, you use the same client with consistent behavior. Concretely, axios. post lets you pass a plain JavaScript object and Axios sets the Content-Type header and stringifies the body for you. A helpful analogy is a mailroom clerk: rather than every developer formatting envelopes and checking delivery receipts, Axios standardizes packaging and returns a status object you can inspect. A common misconception is that Axios hides HTTP entirely; it does not — it surfaces the same HTTP status codes, headers, and bodies but makes them easier to inspect and act on. Example: when a POST returns a created resource, use response. data directly to add it into state instead of parsing the body manually. Final takeaway: Axios reduces repetitive plumbing so you can focus on app logic and robust error handling.

First, install Axios in your React Native project using the package manager you prefer. Once installed, import Axios and use its convenience methods. For a GET request, axios. get returns a promise whose resolved value holds parsed JSON under response. data. For a POST, you can pass a plain object as the body and Axios will set the appropriate header and stringify the payload. An important practical note: always await the axios call inside an async function so errors can be caught with try... catch. Below you will see two short code examples: a terminal install command and minimal GET and POST examples using Axios. The GET example fetches posts and assigns response. data to state. The POST example constructs a JavaScript object and sends it directly. A common mistake is manually calling JSON. stringify or forgetting headers; Axios handles those details for you. Try these snippets in a small screen that shows loading, error, and result states so you can observe response. data directly in your component state. After testing, confirm the network tool shows a request body and a Content-Type header set to application/json.

Robust error handling is one of Axios's biggest practical advantages. When a request fails, Axios may provide three different pieces of information: error. response, error. request, and error. message. error. response exists if the server replied with a status outside the 2xx range; it includes details like status, data, and headers so you can show a specific message for 401 or 500. error. request is present when a request was made but no response was received, indicating network failures or timeouts. error. message covers lower-level issues like misconfigured requests. A recommended pattern is to wrap every awaited call in try... catch and branch inside catch to handle these cases: for error. response read status to decide retry or sign-out flows; for error. request surface a network error UI; otherwise treat it as a request setup issue. A common mistake is checking only error. message or assuming all errors are network errors. Example: when err. response. status equals 401, prompt re-authentication; when err. request is truthy, show a network retry option. Close by logging error. response and error. request during development to learn what your backend returns. Takeaway: differentiate server errors from network and setup errors so your app can respond correctly and communicate useful feedback to users.

Interceptors let you run functions globally before a request is sent or after a response is received. Use a request interceptor to attach headers like Authorization or a custom X-App-Version header, and use a response interceptor to inspect or transform responses and to catch specific status codes like 401 for re-authentication. The process is predictable: the request interceptor receives the config, you modify config. headers as needed, then return config. For responses, return the response to continue the promise chain or inspect error status codes in the response interceptor's error handler. A common use case is adding a request interceptor that reads a token from secure storage and sets the Authorization header. Another use case is logging response. status and response. config. url for telemetry. A key misconception is that interceptors run per component — they run on the Axios instance on which they were registered. That is why creating instance-specific interceptors keeps side effects scoped. Example: add a request interceptor that logs and attaches X-App-Version; then watch the network tool to confirm the header appears on each outgoing request. Final takeaway: interceptors centralize repetitive request and response work so components stay focused on state and rendering.

When your app talks to more than one A P I or when some endpoints need different timeouts and headers, create a custom Axios instance rather than mutating global defaults. Use axios. create with options like baseURL, timeout, and default headers. Then register instance-specific interceptors to scope logging or auth to that A P I only. This prevents accidental side effects when other services require different behavior. For example, set baseURL to the A P I root and a five-second timeout for the users service. In code you import the configured instance and call api. get('/users') rather than axios. get with full URLs. This keeps components cleaner and makes tests simpler because each instance has predictable behavior. A common misconception is that axios. defaults is sufficient — it can be, but it mutates global state and makes isolation harder. Creating instances is a lightweight pattern that improves modularity and reduces unexpected interactions between modules. Try exporting an instance from an api. js file and swapping it into a component to see how code becomes shorter and configuration is centralized. Custom Axios instances for multiple APIs means use axios.create for per-api configurations so headers, timeouts, and interceptors remain scoped and predictable.. In practical terms, keep different api configurations isolated and clear. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
